verses.zh: 有一个患病的人，名叫拉撒路，住在伯大尼，就是马利亚和她姊姊马大的村庄。
verses.en: Now a certain man named Lazarus was sick. He was from Bethany, the village where Mary and her sister Martha lived.[NOTE:1]
notes: Grk “from Bethany, the village of Mary and her sister Martha.”

verses.zh: 这马利亚就是那用香膏抹主，又用头发擦他脚的；患病的拉撒路是她的兄弟。
verses.en: (Now it was Mary who anointed the Lord with perfumed oil[NOTE:1] and wiped his feet dry with her hair, whose brother Lazarus was sick.)[NOTE:2]
notes: Or “perfume,” “ointment.”

This is a parenthetical note by the author. It is a bit surprising that the author here identifies Mary as the one who anointed the Lord with perfumed oil and wiped his feet dry with her hair, since this event is not mentioned until later, in 12:3. Many see this “proleptic” reference as an indication that the author expected his readers to be familiar with the story already, and go on to assume that in general the author in writing the Fourth Gospel assumed his readers were familiar with the other three gospels. Whether the author assumed actual familiarity with the synoptic gospels or not, it is probable that he did assume some familiarity with Mary’s anointing activity.

verses.zh: 她姊妹两个就打发人去见耶稣，说：「主啊，你所爱的人病了。」
verses.en: So the sisters sent a message[NOTE:1] to Jesus,[NOTE:2] “Lord, look, the one you love is sick.”
notes: The phrase “a message” is not in the Greek text but is implied. Direct objects in Greek were often omitted when clear from context.
Grk “to him, saying”; the referent (Jesus) is specified in the translation for clarity.

verses.zh: 耶稣听见，就说：「这病不至于死，乃是为　神的荣耀，叫　神的儿子因此得荣耀。」
verses.en: When Jesus heard this, he said, “This sickness will not lead to death,[NOTE:1] but to God’s glory,[NOTE:2] so that the Son of God may be glorified through it.”[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “This sickness is not to death.”sn Jesus plainly stated the purpose of Lazarus’ sickness in the plan of God: The end of the matter would not be death, but the glorification of the Son. Johannine double-meanings abound here: Even though death would not be the end of the matter, Lazarus is going to die; and ultimately his death and resurrection would lead to the death and resurrection of the Son of God (11:45-53). Furthermore, the glorification of the Son is not praise that comes to him for the miracle, but his death, resurrection, and return to the Father which the miracle precipitates (note the response of the Jewish authorities in 11:47-53).
Or “to God’s praise.”

So that the Son of God may be glorified through it. These statements are highly ironic: For Lazarus, the sickness did not end in his death because he was restored to life. But for Jesus himself, the miraculous sign he performed led to his own death because it confirmed the authorities in their plan to kill Jesus (11:47-53). In the Gospel of John, Jesus’ death is consistently portrayed as his ‘glorification’ through which he accomplishes his return to the Father.

verses.zh: 耶稣素来爱马大和她妹子并拉撒路。
verses.en: (Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus.)[NOTE:1]
notes: This is a parenthetical note by the author. It was necessary for the author to reaffirm Jesus’ love for Martha and her sister and Lazarus here because Jesus’ actions in the following verse appear to be contradictory.

verses.zh: 听见拉撒路病了，就在所居之地仍住了两天。
verses.en: So when he heard that Lazarus[NOTE:1] was sick, he remained in the place where he was for two more days.
notes: Grk “that he”; the referent (Lazarus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

verses.zh: 然后对门徒说：「我们再往犹太去吧。」
verses.en: Then after this, he said to his disciples, “Let us go to Judea again.”[NOTE:1]
notes: The village of Bethany, where Lazarus was, lies in Judea, less than 2 mi (3 km) from Jerusalem (see 11:18).

verses.zh: 门徒说：「拉比，犹太人近来要拿石头打你，你还往那里去吗？」
verses.en: The disciples replied,[NOTE:1] “Rabbi, the Jewish leaders[NOTE:2] were just now trying[NOTE:3] to stone you to death! Are[NOTE:4] you going there again?”
notes: Grk “The disciples said to him.”

Or “the Jewish authorities”; Grk “the Jews.” In NT usage the term ᾿Ιουδαῖοι (Ioudaioi) may refer to the entire Jewish people, the residents of Jerusalem and surrounding territory, the authorities in Jerusalem, or merely those who were hostile to Jesus. (For further information see R. G. Bratcher, “‘The Jews’ in the Gospel of John,” BT 26 [1975]: 401-9.) Here the phrase refers to the Jewish leaders. See the previous references and the notes on the phrase “Jewish people” in v. 19, and “Jewish religious leaders” in vv. 24, 31, 33.
Grk “seeking.”
Grk “And are.” Because of the difference between Greek style, which often begins sentences or clauses with “and,” and English style, which generally does not, καί (kai) has not been translated here.

verses.zh: 耶稣回答说：「白日不是有十二小时吗？人在白日走路，就不至跌倒，因为看见这世上的光。
verses.en: Jesus replied,[NOTE:1] “Are there not 12 hours in a day? If anyone walks around in the daytime, he does not stumble[NOTE:2] because he sees the light of this world.[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “Jesus answered.”
Or “he does not trip.”

What is the light of this world? On one level, of course, it refers to the sun, but the reader of John’s Gospel would recall 8:12 and understand Jesus’ symbolic reference to himself as the light of the world. There is only a limited time left (Are there not 12 hours in a day?) until the Light will be withdrawn (until Jesus returns to the Father) and the one who walks around in the dark will trip and fall (compare the departure of Judas by night in 13:30).

verses.zh: 若在黑夜走路，就必跌倒，因为他没有光。」
verses.en: But if anyone walks around at night,[NOTE:1] he stumbles[NOTE:2] because the light is not in him.”
notes: Grk “in the night.”
Or “he trips.”

verses.zh: 耶稣说了这话，随后对他们说：「我们的朋友拉撒路睡了，我去叫醒他。」
verses.en: After he said this, he added,[NOTE:1] “Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep.[NOTE:2] But I am going there to awaken him.”
notes: Grk “He said these things, and after this he said to them.”

The verb κοιμάω (koimaō) literally means “sleep,” but it is often used in the Bible as a euphemism for death when speaking of believers. This metaphorical usage by its very nature emphasizes the hope of resurrection: Believers will one day “wake up” out of death. Here the term refers to death, but “asleep” was used in the translation to emphasize the metaphorical, rhetorical usage of the term, especially in light of the disciples’ confusion over what Jesus actually meant (see v. 13).

verses.zh: 门徒说：「主啊，他若睡了，就必好了。」
verses.en: Then the disciples replied,[NOTE:1] “Lord, if he has fallen asleep, he will recover.”
notes: Grk “Then the disciples said to him.”

verses.zh: 耶稣这话是指着他死说的，他们却以为是说照常睡了。
verses.en: (Now Jesus had been talking about[NOTE:1] his death, but they[NOTE:2] thought he had been talking about real sleep.)[NOTE:3]
notes: Or “speaking about.”
Grk “these.”
This is a parenthetical note by the author.tn Grk “the sleep of slumber”; this is a redundant expression to emphasize physical sleep as opposed to death.

verses.zh: 耶稣就明明地告诉他们说：「拉撒路死了。
verses.en: Then Jesus told them plainly, “Lazarus has died,

verses.zh: 我没有在那里就欢喜，这是为你们的缘故，好叫你们相信。如今我们可以往他那里去吧。」
verses.en: and I am glad[NOTE:1] for your sake that I was not there, so that you may believe.[NOTE:2] But let us go to him.”
notes: Grk “and I rejoice.”

So that you may believe. Why does Jesus make this statement? It seems necessary to understand the disciples’ belief here in a developmental sense because there are numerous references to the disciples’ faith previous to this in John’s Gospel, notably 2:11. Their concept of who Jesus really was is continually being expanded and challenged; they are undergoing spiritual growth; the climax is reached in the confession of Thomas in John 20:28.

verses.zh: 多马，又称为低土马，就对那同作门徒的说：「我们也去和他同死吧。」
verses.en: So Thomas (called Didymus[NOTE:1])[NOTE:2] said to his fellow disciples, “Let us go too, so that we may die with him.”[NOTE:3]
notes: Didymus means “the twin” in Greek.
This is a parenthetical note by the author.

One gets the impression from Thomas’ statement “Let us go too, so that we may die with him” that he was something of a pessimist resigned to his fate. And yet his dedicated loyalty to Jesus and his determination to accompany him at all costs was truly commendable. Nor is the contrast between this statement and the confession of Thomas in 20:28, which forms the climax of the entire Fourth Gospel, to be overlooked; certainly Thomas’ concept of who Jesus is has changed drastically between 11:16 and 20:28.

verses.zh: 耶稣到了，就知道拉撒路在坟墓里已经四天了。
verses.en: When[NOTE:1] Jesus arrived,[NOTE:2] he found that Lazarus[NOTE:3] had been in the tomb four days already.[NOTE:4]
notes: Grk “Then when.”
Grk “came.”
Grk “he”; the referent (Lazarus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

Grk “he had already had four days in the tomb” (an idiom).sn There is no description of the journey itself. The author simply states that when Jesus arrived, he found that Lazarus had been in the tomb four days already. He had died some time before this but probably not very long (cf. Ananias and Sapphira in Acts 5:6, 10 who were buried immediately after they died, as was the common practice of the time). There is some later evidence (early 3rd century) of a rabbinic belief that the soul hovered near the body of the deceased for three days, hoping to be able to return to the body. But on the fourth day it saw the beginning of decomposition and finally departed (Leviticus Rabbah 18.1). If this belief is as old as the 1st century, it might suggest the significance of the four days: After this time, resurrection would be a first-order miracle, an unequivocal demonstration of the power of God. It is not certain if the tradition is this early, but it is suggestive. Certainly the author does not appear to attach any symbolic significance to the four days in the narrative.

verses.zh: 伯大尼离耶路撒冷不远，约有六里路。
verses.en: (Now Bethany was less than two miles[NOTE:1] from Jerusalem,[NOTE:2]
notes: Or “three kilometers”; Grk “fifteen stades” (a stade as a unit of linear measure is about 607 feet or 185 meters).
For location see Map5-B1; Map6-F3; Map7-E2; Map8-F2; Map10-B3; JP1-F4; JP2-F4; JP3-F4; JP4-F4.

verses.zh: 有好些犹太人来看马大和马利亚，要为她们的兄弟安慰她们。
verses.en: so many of the Jewish people of the region[NOTE:1] had come to Martha and Mary to console them[NOTE:2] over the loss of their brother.)[NOTE:3]
notes: Or “many of the Judeans” (cf. BDAG 479 s.v. ᾿Ιουδαῖος 2.e); Grk “many of the Jews.” Here the phrase refers to the residents of Jerusalem and the surrounding area in general (those who had been friends or relatives of Lazarus or his sisters would mainly be in view) since the Jewish religious authorities (“the chief priests and the Pharisees”) are specifically mentioned as a separate group in John 11:46-47. See also the note on the phrase “the Jewish leaders” in v. 8.
Or “to comfort them” or “to offer them sympathy.”
Grk “to comfort them concerning their brother”; the words “loss of” are not in the Greek text but are implied.sn This is a parenthetical note by the author.

verses.zh: 马大听见耶稣来了，就出去迎接他；马利亚却仍然坐在家里。
verses.en: So when Martha heard that Jesus was coming, she went out to meet him, but Mary was sitting in the house.[NOTE:1]
notes: Notice the difference in the response of the two sisters: Martha went out to meet Jesus, while Mary remains sitting in the house. It is similar to the incident in Luke 10:38-42. Here again one finds Martha occupied with the responsibilities of hospitality; she is the one who greets Jesus.

verses.zh: 马大对耶稣说：「主啊，你若早在这里，我兄弟必不死。
verses.en: Martha[NOTE:1] said to Jesus, “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.
notes: Grk “Then Martha.” Here οὖν (oun) has not been translated for stylistic reasons.

verses.zh: 就是现在，我也知道，你无论向　神求甚么，　神也必赐给你。」
verses.en: But even now I know that whatever you ask from God, God will grant[NOTE:1] you.”[NOTE:2]
notes: Or “give.”

The statement “whatever you ask from God, God will grant you” by Martha presents something of a dilemma because she seems to be suggesting here (implicitly at least) the possibility of a resurrection for her brother. However, Martha’s statement in 11:39 makes it clear that she had no idea that a resurrection was still possible. How then are her words in 11:22 to be understood? It seems best to take them as a confession of Martha’s continuing faith in Jesus even though he was not there in time to help her brother. She means, in effect, “Even though you weren’t here in time to help, I still believe that God grants your requests.”

verses.zh: 耶稣说：「你兄弟必然复活。」
verses.en: Jesus replied,[NOTE:1] “Your brother will come back to life again.”[NOTE:2]
notes: Grk “Jesus said to her.”

Or “Your brother will rise again.”sn Jesus’ remark to Martha that Lazarus would come back to life again is another example of the misunderstood statement. Martha apparently took it as a customary statement of consolation and joined Jesus in professing belief in the general resurrection of the body at the end of the age. However, as Jesus went on to point out in 11:25-26, Martha’s general understanding of the resurrection at the last day was inadequate for the present situation, for the gift of life that conquers death was a present reality to Jesus. This is consistent with the author’s perspective on eternal life in the Fourth Gospel: It is not only a future reality, but something to be experienced in the present as well. It is also consistent with the so-called “realized eschatology” of the Fourth Gospel.

verses.zh: 马大说：「我知道在末日复活的时候，他必复活。」
verses.en: Martha said,[NOTE:1] “I know that he will come back to life again[NOTE:2] in the resurrection at the last day.”
notes: Grk “Martha said to him.”
Or “will rise again.”

verses.zh: 耶稣对她说：「复活在我，生命也在我。信我的人虽然死了，也必复活；
verses.en: Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. The one who believes in me will live[NOTE:1] even if he dies,
notes: That is, will come to life.

verses.zh: 凡活着信我的人必永远不死。你信这话吗？」
verses.en: and the one who lives and believes in me will never die.[NOTE:1] Do you believe this?”
notes: Grk “will never die forever.”

verses.zh: 马大说：「主啊，是的，我信你是基督，是　神的儿子，就是那要临到世界的。」
verses.en: She replied,[NOTE:1] “Yes, Lord, I believe[NOTE:2] that you are the Christ,[NOTE:3] the Son of God who comes into the world.”[NOTE:4]
notes: Grk “She said to him.”

The perfect tense in Greek is often used to emphasize the results or present state of a past action. Such is the case here. To emphasize this nuance the perfect tense verb πεπίστευκα (pepisteuka) has been translated as a present tense. This is in keeping with the present context, where Jesus asks of her present state of belief in v. 26, and the theology of the Gospel as a whole, which emphasizes the continuing effects and present reality of faith. For discussion on this use of the perfect tense, see ExSyn 574-76 and B. M. Fanning, Verbal Aspect, 291-97.
Or “the Messiah” (Both Greek “Christ” and Hebrew and Aramaic “Messiah” mean “one who has been anointed”).sn See the note on Christ in 1:20.
Or “the Son of God, the one who comes into the world.”

verses.zh: 马大说了这话，就回去暗暗地叫她妹子马利亚，说：「夫子来了，叫你。」
verses.en: And when she had said this, Martha[NOTE:1] went and called her sister Mary, saying privately,[NOTE:2] “The Teacher is here and is asking for you.”[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “she”; the referent (Martha) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Or “in secret” (as opposed to publicly, so that the other mourners did not hear).
Grk “is calling you.”

verses.zh: 马利亚听见了，就急忙起来，到耶稣那里去。
verses.en: So when Mary[NOTE:1] heard this, she got up quickly and went to him.
notes: Grk “she”; the referent (Mary) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

verses.zh: 那时，耶稣还没有进村子，仍在马大迎接他的地方。
verses.en: (Now Jesus had not yet entered the village, but was still in the place where Martha had come out to meet him.)

verses.zh: 那些同马利亚在家里安慰她的犹太人，见她急忙起来出去，就跟着她，以为她要往坟墓那里去哭。
verses.en: Then the people[NOTE:1] who were with Mary[NOTE:2] in the house consoling her saw her[NOTE:3] get up quickly and go out. They followed her because they thought she was going to the tomb to weep[NOTE:4] there.
notes: Or “the Judeans”; Grk “the Jews.” Here the phrase refers to the friends, acquaintances, and relatives of Lazarus or his sisters who had come to mourn, since the Jewish religious authorities are specifically mentioned as a separate group in John 11:46-47. See also the notes on the phrase “the Jewish leaders” in v. 8 and “the Jewish people of the region” in v. 19.
Grk “her”; the referent (Mary) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Grk “Mary”; the proper name (Mary) has been replaced with the pronoun (her) in keeping with conventional English style, to avoid repetition.
Or “to mourn” (referring to the loud wailing or crying typical of public mourning in that culture).

verses.zh: 马利亚到了耶稣那里，看见他，就俯伏在他脚前，说：「主啊，你若早在这里，我兄弟必不死。」
verses.en: Now when Mary came to the place where Jesus was and saw him, she fell at his feet and said to him, “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.”

verses.zh: 耶稣看见她哭，并看见与她同来的犹太人也哭，就心里悲叹，又甚忧愁，
verses.en: When Jesus saw her weeping, and the people[NOTE:1] who had come with her weeping, he was intensely moved[NOTE:2] in spirit and greatly distressed.[NOTE:3]
notes: Or “the Judeans”; Grk “the Jews.” Here the phrase refers to the friends, acquaintances, and relatives of Lazarus or his sisters who had come to mourn, since the Jewish religious authorities are specifically mentioned as a separate group in John 11:46-47. See also the notes on the phrase “the Jewish leaders” in v. 8, “the Jewish people of the region” in v. 19, and the word “people” in v. 31.

Or (perhaps) “he was deeply indignant.” The verb ἐνεβριμήσατο (enebrimēsato), which is repeated in John 11:38, indicates a strong display of emotion, somewhat difficult to translate—“shuddered, moved with the deepest emotions.” In the LXX, the verb and its cognates are used to describe a display of indignation (Dan 11:30, for example—see also Mark 14:5). Jesus displayed this reaction to the afflicted in Mark 1:43, Matt 9:30. Was he angry at the afflicted? No, but he was angry because he found himself face-to-face with the manifestations of Satan’s kingdom of evil. Here, the realm of Satan was represented by death.

Or “greatly troubled.” The verb ταράσσω (tarassō) also occurs in similar contexts to those of ἐνεβριμήσατο (enebrimēsato). John uses it in 14:1 and 27 to describe the reaction of the disciples to the imminent death of Jesus, and in 13:21 the verb describes how Jesus reacted to the thought of being betrayed by Judas, into whose heart Satan had entered.

verses.zh: 便说：「你们把他安放在哪里？」他们回答说：「请主来看。」
verses.en: He asked,[NOTE:1] “Where have you laid him?”[NOTE:2] They replied,[NOTE:3] “Lord, come and see.”
notes: Grk “And he said.” Because of the difference between Greek style, which often begins sentences or clauses with “and,” and English style, which generally does not, καί (kai) has not been translated here.
Or “Where have you placed him?”
Grk “They said to him.” The indirect object αὐτῷ (autō) has not been translated here for stylistic reasons.

verses.zh: 耶稣哭了。
verses.en: Jesus wept.[NOTE:1]
notes: Jesus wept. The Greek word used here for Jesus’ weeping (ἐδάκρυσεν, edakrusen) is different from the one used to describe the weeping of Mary and the Jews in v. 33 which indicated loud wailing and cries of lament. This word simply means “to shed tears” and has more the idea of quiet grief. But why did Jesus do this? Not out of grief for Lazarus, since he was about to be raised to life again. L. Morris (John [NICNT], 558) thinks it was grief over the misconception of those round about. But it seems that in the context the weeping is triggered by the thought of Lazarus in the tomb: This was not personal grief over the loss of a friend (since Lazarus was about to be restored to life) but grief over the effects of sin, death, and the realm of Satan. It was a natural complement to the previous emotional expression of anger (11:33). It is also possible that Jesus wept at the tomb of Lazarus because he knew there was also a tomb for himself ahead.

verses.zh: 犹太人就说：「你看他爱这人是何等恳切。」
verses.en: Thus the people who had come to mourn[NOTE:1] said, “Look how much he loved him!”
notes: Or “the Judeans”; Grk “the Jews.” Here the phrase refers to the friends, acquaintances, and relatives of Lazarus or his sisters who had come to mourn, since the Jewish religious authorities are specifically mentioned as a separate group in John 11:46-47. See also the notes on the phrase “the Jewish leaders” in v. 8 and “the Jewish people of the region” in v. 19, as well as the notes on the word “people” in vv. 31, 33.

verses.zh: 其中有人说：「他既然开了瞎子的眼睛，岂不能叫这人不死吗？」
verses.en: But some of them said, “This is the man who caused the blind man to see![NOTE:1] Couldn’t he have done something to keep Lazarus[NOTE:2] from dying?”
notes: Grk “who opened the eyes of the blind man” (“opening the eyes” is an idiom referring to restoration of sight).

Grk “this one”; the second half of 11:37 reads Grk “Could not this one who opened the eyes of the blind have done something to keep this one from dying?” In the Greek text the repetition of “this one” in 11:37b referring to two different persons (first Jesus, second Lazarus) could confuse a modern reader. Thus the first reference, to Jesus, has been translated as “he” to refer back to the beginning of v. 37, where the reference to “the man who caused the blind man to see” is clearly a reference to Jesus. The second reference, to Lazarus, has been specified (“Lazarus”) in the translation for clarity.

verses.zh: 耶稣又心里悲叹，来到坟墓前；那坟墓是个洞，有一块石头挡着。
verses.en: Jesus, intensely moved[NOTE:1] again, came to the tomb. (Now it was a cave, and a stone was placed across it.)[NOTE:2]
notes: Or (perhaps) “Jesus was deeply indignant.”
This is a parenthetical note by the author.

verses.zh: 耶稣说：「你们把石头挪开。」那死人的姊姊马大对他说：「主啊，他现在必是臭了，因为他死了已经四天了。」
verses.en: Jesus said, “Take away the stone.”[NOTE:1] Martha, the sister of the deceased,[NOTE:2] replied, “Lord, by this time the body will have a bad smell[NOTE:3] because he has been buried[NOTE:4] four days.”[NOTE:5]
notes: Or “Remove the stone.”
Grk “the sister of the one who had died.”
Grk “already he stinks.”
Or “been there” (in the tomb—see John 11:17).

He has been buried four days. Although all the details of the miracle itself are not given, those details which are mentioned are important. The statement made by Martha is extremely significant for understanding what actually took place. There is no doubt that Lazarus had really died because the decomposition of his body had already begun to take place, since he had been dead for four days.

verses.zh: 耶稣说：「我不是对你说过，你若信，就必看见　神的荣耀吗？」
verses.en: Jesus responded,[NOTE:1] “Didn’t I tell you that if you believe, you would see the glory of God?”
notes: Grk “Jesus said to her.”

verses.zh: 他们就把石头挪开。耶稣举目望天，说：「父啊，我感谢你，因为你已经听我。
verses.en: So they took away[NOTE:1] the stone. Jesus looked upward[NOTE:2] and said, “Father, I thank you that you have listened to me.[NOTE:3]
notes: Or “they removed.”
Grk “lifted up his eyes above.”
Or “that you have heard me.”

verses.zh: 我也知道你常听我，但我说这话是为周围站着的众人，叫他们信是你差了我来。」
verses.en: I knew that you always listen to me,[NOTE:1] but I said this[NOTE:2] for the sake of the crowd standing around here, that they may believe that you sent me.”
notes: Grk “that you always hear me.”
The word “this” is not in the Greek text. Direct objects in Greek were often omitted when clear from the context.

verses.zh: 说了这话，就大声呼叫说：「拉撒路出来！」
verses.en: When[NOTE:1] he had said this, he shouted in a loud voice,[NOTE:2] “Lazarus, come out!”
notes: Grk “And when.”
The purpose of the loud voice was probably to ensure that all in the crowd could hear (compare the purpose of the prayer of thanksgiving in vv. 41-42).

verses.zh: 那死人就出来了，手脚裹着布，脸上包着手巾。耶稣对他们说：「解开，叫他走！」
verses.en: The one who had died came out, his feet and hands tied up with strips of cloth,[NOTE:1] and a cloth wrapped around his face.[NOTE:2] Jesus said to them, “Unwrap him[NOTE:3] and let him go.”
notes: Many have wondered how Lazarus got out of the tomb if his hands and feet were still tied up with strips of cloth. The author does not tell, and with a miracle of this magnitude, this is not an important fact to know. If Lazarus’ decomposing body was brought back to life by the power of God, then it could certainly have been moved out of the tomb by that same power. Others have suggested that the legs were bound separately, which would remove the difficulty, but the account gives no indication of this. What may be of more significance for the author is the comparison which this picture naturally evokes with the resurrection of Jesus, where the graveclothes stayed in the tomb neatly folded (20:6-7). Jesus, unlike Lazarus, would never need graveclothes again.
Grk “and his face tied around with cloth.”
Grk “Loose him.”

verses.zh: 那些来看马利亚的犹太人见了耶稣所做的事，就多有信他的；
verses.en: Then many of the people,[NOTE:1] who had come with Mary and had seen the things Jesus[NOTE:2] did, believed in him.
notes: Or “the Judeans”; Grk “the Jews.” Here the phrase refers to the friends, acquaintances, and relatives of Lazarus or his sisters who had come to mourn, since the Jewish religious authorities are specifically mentioned as a separate group in John 11:46-47. See also the notes on the phrase “the Jewish leaders” in v. 8 and “the Jewish people of the region” in v. 19, as well as the notes on the word “people” in vv. 31, 33 and the phrase “people who had come to mourn” in v. 36.
Grk “he”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

verses.zh: 但其中也有去见法利赛人的，将耶稣所做的事告诉他们。
verses.en: But some of them went to the Pharisees[NOTE:1] and reported to them[NOTE:2] what Jesus had done.
notes: See the note on Pharisees in 1:24.
Grk “told them.”

verses.zh: 祭司长和法利赛人聚集公会，说：「这人行好些神迹，我们怎么办呢？
verses.en: So the chief priests and the Pharisees[NOTE:1] called the council[NOTE:2] together and said, “What are we doing? For this man is performing many miraculous signs.
notes: The phrase “chief priests and Pharisees” is a comprehensive name for the groups represented in the ruling council (the Sanhedrin) as in John 7:45; 18:3; Acts 5:22, 26.

Or “Sanhedrin” (the Sanhedrin was the highest legal, legislative, and judicial body among the Jews). The συνέδριον (sunedrion) which they gathered was probably an informal meeting rather than the official Sanhedrin. This is the only occurrence of the word συνέδριον in the Gospel of John, and the only anarthrous singular use in the NT. There are other plural anarthrous uses which have the general meaning “councils.” The fact that Caiaphas in 11:49 is referred to as “one of them” supports the unofficial nature of the meeting; in the official Sanhedrin he, being high priest that year, would have presided over the assembly. Thus it appears that an informal council was called to discuss what to do about Jesus and his activities.

verses.zh: 若这样由着他，人人都要信他，罗马人也要来夺我们的地土和我们的百姓。」
verses.en: If we allow him to go on in this way,[NOTE:1] everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away our sanctuary[NOTE:2] and our nation.”
notes: Grk “If we let him do thus.”
Or “holy place”; Grk “our place” (a reference to the temple in Jerusalem).

verses.zh: 内中有一个人，名叫该亚法，本年作大祭司，对他们说：「你们不知道甚么。
verses.en: Then one of them, Caiaphas, who was high priest that year, said,[NOTE:1] “You know nothing at all!
notes: Grk “said to them.” The indirect object αὐτοῖς (autois) has not been translated for stylistic reasons.

verses.zh: 独不想一个人替百姓死，免得通国灭亡，就是你们的益处。」
verses.en: You do not realize[NOTE:1] that it is more to your advantage to have one man[NOTE:2] die for the people than for the whole nation to perish.”[NOTE:3]
notes: Or “you are not considering.”

Although it is possible to argue that ἄνθρωπος (anthrōpos) should be translated “person” here since it is not necessarily masculinity that is in view in Caiaphas’ statement, “man” was retained in the translation because in 11:47 “this man” (οὗτος ὁ ἄνθρωπος, outos ho anthrōpos) has as its referent a specific individual, Jesus, and it was felt this connection should be maintained.

In his own mind Caiaphas was no doubt giving voice to a common-sense statement of political expediency. Yet he was unconsciously echoing a saying of Jesus himself (cf. Mark 10:45). Caiaphas was right; the death of Jesus would save the nation from destruction. Yet Caiaphas could not suspect that Jesus would die, not in place of the political nation Israel, but on behalf of the true people of God; and he would save them, not from physical destruction, but from eternal destruction (cf. 3:16-17). The understanding of Caiaphas’ words in a sense that Caiaphas could not possibly have imagined at the time he uttered them serves as a clear example of the way in which the author understood that words and actions could be invested retrospectively with a meaning not consciously intended or understood by those present at the time.

verses.zh: 他这话不是出于自己，是因他本年作大祭司，所以预言耶稣将要替这一国死；
verses.en: (Now he did not say this on his own,[NOTE:1] but because he was high priest that year, he prophesied that Jesus was going to die for the Jewish nation,[NOTE:2]
notes: Grk “say this from himself.”
The word “Jewish” is not in the Greek text, but is clearly implied by the context (so also NIV; TEV “the Jewish people”).

verses.zh: 也不但替这一国死，并要将　神四散的子民都聚集归一。
verses.en: and not for the Jewish nation[NOTE:1] only,[NOTE:2] but to gather together[NOTE:3] into one the children of God who are scattered.)[NOTE:4]
notes: See the note on the word “nation” in the previous verse.

The author in his comment expands the prophecy to include the Gentiles (not for the Jewish nation only), a confirmation that the Fourth Gospel was directed, at least partly, to a Gentile audience. There are echoes of Pauline concepts here (particularly Eph 2:11-22) in the stress on the unity of Jew and Gentile.
Grk “that he might gather together.”
This is a parenthetical note by the author.

verses.zh: 从那日起，他们就商议要杀耶稣。
verses.en: So from that day they planned together to kill him.

verses.zh: 所以，耶稣不再显然行在犹太人中间，就离开那里往靠近旷野的地方去，到了一座城，名叫以法莲，就在那里和门徒同住。
verses.en: Thus Jesus no longer went[NOTE:1] around publicly[NOTE:2] among the Judeans,[NOTE:3] but went away from there to the region near the wilderness, to a town called Ephraim,[NOTE:4] and stayed there with his disciples.
notes: Grk “walked.”
Or “openly.”

Grk “among the Jews.” Here the phrase refers to the residents of Judea in general, who would be likely to report Jesus to the religious authorities. The vicinity around Jerusalem was no longer safe for Jesus and his disciples. On the translation “Judeans” cf. BDAG 479 s.v. ᾿Ιουδαῖος 2.e. See also the references in vv. 8, 19, 31, 33, 36, and 45.

There is no certain identification of the location to which Jesus withdrew in response to the decision of the Jewish authorities. Many have suggested the present town of Et-Taiyibeh, identified with ancient Ophrah (Josh 18:23) or Ephron (Josh 15:9). If so, this would be 12-15 mi (19-24 km) northeast of Jerusalem.

verses.zh: 犹太人的逾越节近了，有许多人从乡下上耶路撒冷去，要在节前洁净自己。
verses.en: Now the Jewish Feast of Passover[NOTE:1] was near, and many people went up to Jerusalem[NOTE:2] from the rural areas before the Passover to cleanse themselves ritually.[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “the Passover of the Jews.” This is the final Passover of Jesus’ ministry. The author is now on the eve of the week of the Passion. Some time prior to the feast itself, Jerusalem would be crowded with pilgrims from the surrounding districts (ἐκ τῆς χώρας, ek tēs chōras) who had come to purify themselves ceremonially before the feast.
For location see Map5-B1; Map6-F3; Map7-E2; Map8-F2; Map10-B3; JP1-F4; JP2-F4; JP3-F4; JP4-F4.
Or “to purify themselves” (to undergo or carry out ceremonial cleansing before participating in the Passover celebration).

verses.zh: 他们就寻找耶稣，站在殿里彼此说：「你们的意思如何，他不来过节吗？」
verses.en: Thus they were looking for Jesus,[NOTE:1] and saying to one another as they stood in the temple courts,[NOTE:2] “What do you think? That he won’t come to the feast?”
notes: Grk “they were seeking Jesus.”
Grk “in the temple.”

verses.zh: 那时，祭司长和法利赛人早已吩咐说，若有人知道耶稣在哪里，就要报明，好去拿他。
verses.en: (Now the chief priests and the Pharisees[NOTE:1] had given orders that anyone who knew where Jesus[NOTE:2] was should report it, so that they could arrest[NOTE:3] him.)[NOTE:4]
notes: The phrase “chief priests and Pharisees” is a comprehensive name for the groups represented in the ruling council (the Sanhedrin) as in John 7:45; 18:3; Acts 5:22, 26.
Grk “he”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Or “could seize.”
This is a parenthetical note by the author.
